stories.title: Claude Tag: Multiplayer, Proactive, Persistent Agents in Slack
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Claude is getting a Slack integration that supports multiplayer, proactive, and persistent agent behavior — meaning it can operate across conversations, respond to triggers without being explicitly summoned, and maintain context over time within Slack workspaces.

↳ THE REAL STORY
This is a meaningful shift from the typical chatbot-in-a-channel pattern. Persistent context means Claude can track a thread of work across days, not just a single session. Proactive behavior means it can surface information or act on conditions without a human typing a slash command. Multiplayer means multiple teammates can interact with the same agent instance — shared state, not isolated DMs. For teams already living in Slack, this could replace a class of lightweight automation that currently requires Zapier, custom bots, or n8n pipelines.
stories.considerations: The catch is trust and auditability. Proactive agents that act without explicit prompts in a shared workspace raise immediate questions: who authorized that action, what data did it read, and can you replay the decision log? Anthropic hasn't published details on permission scoping or audit trails for this integration. Until those are clear, putting this anywhere near sensitive channels — HR, legal, finance — would be premature. Watch for how workspace admins can constrain what Claude can see and do, not just what it can say.

stories.title: datasette 1.0a35
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Datasette 1.0a35 ships with a new "Create table" UI in the database actions menu, backed by a dedicated `/<database>/-/create` API endpoint — part of a larger alpha release Simon Willison flags as significant enough to warrant a separate write-up.

↳ THE REAL STORY
For developers using Datasette as a lightweight data management layer, a native table-creation interface means less reliance on external SQLite tooling or raw SQL just to scaffold a schema. The `/<database>/-/create` endpoint also opens the door to programmatic table creation via HTTP — useful for pipelines that need to spin up tables dynamically without dropping into a SQLite client. The excerpt cuts off before the other two highlights, but Willison's "big release" framing on an alpha suggests meaningful API surface changes are accumulating ahead of the eventual 1.0 stable.
stories.considerations: The project has been in alpha for a long time — 1.0a35 means at least 35 alpha releases. That's not a knock on the quality, but anyone building production tooling on top of Datasette's API surface should note that "alpha" here means the API contract is still explicitly unstable. The new `/-/create` endpoint could change shape before 1.0 lands. Worth checking the full release notes once Willison publishes his follow-up tomorrow before wiring this into anything load-bearing.

stories.title: OPFS + Pyodide test harness
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Simon Willison built a browser-based test harness combining OPFS (Origin Private File System) and Pyodide to explore whether Python code running in WebAssembly can read and write persistent SQLite files directly in the browser — no server required.

↳ THE REAL STORY
This is groundwork for Datasette Lite potentially gaining persistent storage. Right now, Datasette Lite runs a full Python data analysis stack in the browser but loses everything on page reload. If OPFS + Pyodide can be wired together reliably, users could open a local SQLite file, query and edit it with Datasette's full interface, and have changes persist — all client-side. The test harness is Willison stress-testing the plumbing before committing to the integration: can Pyodide's file system layer actually talk to the browser's OPFS API without corruption or permission friction?
stories.considerations: OPFS is still unevenly supported and its behavior inside SharedArrayBuffer-dependent environments like Pyodide gets complicated fast — especially around worker thread access and file locking. SQLite's WAL mode adds another layer of potential conflict when the same file is touched by both the OPFS layer and Pyodide's virtual FS. This harness will tell Willison whether the happy path works; the harder question is whether edge cases (concurrent access, large files, browser tab suspension) are tractable enough to ship to real users.
